candidates.next_evidence: Track customer concentration, realized utilization, capex funding cost, GPU depreciation assumptions, gross margin trajectory, backlog conversion, and whether contracted capacity is take-or-pay versus usage-sensitive.
candidates.node_relation: Direct demand-side and capacity-provider exposure: sells contracted AI compute capacity to hyperscalers, AI labs, and enterprise inference/training customers.
candidates.theme_relation: If hyperscaler and AI-lab demand remains supply-constrained, CoreWeave backlog and GPU-backed financing are direct evidence of monetizable AI compute demand; if utilization or customer concentration weakens, it becomes an overbuild-risk signal.
candidates.why_include: CoreWeave reported nearly $100B of revenue backlog as of March 31, 2026 and separately announced a long-term Meta AI cloud capacity agreement through 2032 for about $21B, making it one of the clearest public-market mappings to outsourced AI compute demand.

candidates.next_evidence: Verify AI-specific share of bookings, power availability by market, pre-leasing of development pipeline, lease terms, customer credit quality, construction yields, and delays from grid interconnection or equipment bottlenecks.
candidates.node_relation: Scarce data-center capacity provider: leases hyperscale and interconnection-rich data-center capacity to cloud, AI, and enterprise customers.
candidates.theme_relation: Hyperscaler AI capex translates into demand for powered shells, interconnection, metro capacity, and signed-but-not-commenced leases; Digital Realty’s bookings/backlog are a physical-capacity check on the cloud compute cycle.
candidates.why_include: Digital Realty reported Q1 2026 record bookings expected to generate $707M of annualized GAAP rental revenue at 100% share and a total backlog of $1.8B of annualized GAAP base rent, while management cited acceleration in data-center demand and its largest hyperscale lease in company history.

candidates.next_evidence: Quantify data-center revenue mix, hyperscaler/customer exposure, margin sustainability, labor availability, safety/quality execution risk, cancellation clauses, and whether backlog converts without cost overruns.
candidates.node_relation: Buildout execution bottleneck: provides scarce skilled labor and mechanical/electrical contracting needed to turn hyperscaler capex into operational data-center capacity.
candidates.theme_relation: AI data-center demand stresses not only chips and power but also construction labor, mechanical systems, electrical installation, commissioning, and project execution capacity.
candidates.why_include: Comfort Systems USA reported Q1 2026 backlog of $12.45B, up from $6.89B a year earlier, with 51% organic revenue growth. Prior filings explicitly tied technology-sector revenue strength particularly to data centers, making it a credible second-order AI capex beneficiary.

candidates.next_evidence: Identify customer concentration, delivery schedule, profitability of the $4B capacity agreement, manufacturing expansion risks, component constraints such as fans/pumps/heat exchangers, and whether demand is direct-to-chip liquid cooling or broader HVAC.
candidates.node_relation: Cooling equipment and thermal-management supplier: exposed to liquid/air cooling demand from high-density AI data-center deployments.
candidates.theme_relation: AI rack densities create thermal bottlenecks; hyperscaler capex can flow to cooling vendors before compute capacity can be deployed.
candidates.why_include: Modine announced a long-term capacity agreement through 2029 with a strategic data-center customer for Airedale by Modine cooling solutions, valued at approximately $4B, and has been reorganizing around a dedicated Data Centers segment.

candidates.next_evidence: Check fuel supply economics, permitting, deployment timing, warranty/service costs, customer concentration, financing needs, emissions/regulatory treatment, and whether onsite generation competes with or complements utility-scale power deals.
candidates.node_relation: Regulated-input workaround and onsite power supplier: provides fuel-cell systems that can reduce grid-interconnection dependence for data centers and AI/cloud infrastructure.
candidates.theme_relation: If grid interconnection, power availability, and utility delays constrain hyperscaler AI capex, onsite power becomes a scarce enabling layer; Bloom’s Oracle agreement is a direct AI/cloud infrastructure proof point.
candidates.why_include: Bloom Energy announced an expanded Oracle partnership under which Oracle intends to procure up to 2.8GW of Bloom fuel-cell capacity, including an initial 1.2GW contracted and deploying across U.S. projects to support AI and cloud infrastructure.

node: Hyperscaler AI capex and cloud compute demand
summary: Expanded the universe around the hyperscaler AI capex/cloud-demand node toward public companies exposed to scarce capacity, buildout execution, cooling, power, and contracted AI-cloud demand. The five highest-relevance additions for this pass are CoreWeave as a newly public AI cloud capacity provider, Digital Realty as a hyperscale/AI data-center capacity owner, Comfort Systems USA as a scarce mechanical/electrical contractor, Modine as a data-center cooling supplier with a large capacity agreement, and Bloom Energy as an onsite power supplier to AI/cloud data-center projects. These are research candidates only, not trading recommendations.
